content: Cefepime is a cephalosporin antibiotic used to treat a wide range of bacterial infections. It is administered via injection into a muscle or vein as directed by a healthcare provider. The dosage is determined based on the patient’s medical condition and response to treatment. If used at home, patients must be trained on proper preparation and administration techniques by a healthcare professional. Before use, the solution should be visually inspected for particles or discoloration; if present, the medication should not be used. Frozen pre-mixed solutions should be thawed at room temperature or in a refrigerator, but not in a water bath or microwave. After thawing, the bag should be shaken well and checked for leaks. Leaking bags should be discarded. Cefepime should be taken at evenly spaced intervals for the full prescribed duration, even if symptoms improve after a few days. Stopping the medication prematurely may result in a return of the infection. Common side effects include swelling, redness, or pain at the injection site. While rare, cefepime may cause a severe intestinal condition due to Clostridioides difficile (C. difficile) infection, which can occur during or even weeks to months after treatment. Prolonged or repeated use of cefepime may lead to oral thrush or a new yeast infection. Serious allergic reactions are rare but possible. Patients should immediately report any severe side effects to their healthcare provider. Cefepime may interact with other medications, potentially altering their effects or increasing the risk of side effects. For example, it can increase the nephrotoxic and/or ototoxic effects of aminoglycosides like streptomycin and tobramycin. It may also reduce the efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors such as tislelizumab and toripalimab. Additionally, cefepime can decrease the effectiveness of live bacterial vaccines, such as the typhoid vaccine, due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Live bacterial vaccines should be administered only after completing cefepime treatment. Cefepime may also increase the effects of warfarin, potentially reducing prothrombin activity, and should be used cautiously in such cases. Patients should inform their healthcare provider of any allergies, particularly to cephalosporins, penicillins, or other antibiotics, as well as any other medical conditions or medications they are taking. Cefepime passes into breast milk in small amounts but is unlikely to harm a nursing infant. The benefits of breastfeeding should be weighed against the mother’s clinical need for cefepime and any potential risks to the infant. Cefepime is minimally metabolized in the liver and primarily excreted unchanged in the urine. Its half-life is approximately 2 hours, and it has a volume of distribution of 16–20 liters in adults. It penetrates inflammatory fluids at concentrations around 80% of serum levels and bronchial mucosa at approximately 60% of plasma levels. Protein binding is low, at 16–19%. Patients should store cefepime as instructed by their pharmacist and properly discard expired or unused medication. It should not be flushed down the toilet or poured into a drain unless directed to do so. In case of overdose, immediate medical attention is required. In the U.S., patients can contact the Poison Control Center at 1-800-222-1222, and in Canada, they can call 1-844-764-7669. Regular laboratory tests, such as complete blood counts and kidney function tests, may be necessary during treatment to monitor for potential side effects or complications. This information is not exhaustive and does not replace professional medical advice. Patients should always consult their healthcare provider for personalized guidance regarding cefepime and their specific health needs.
